references.text: Moses receives the command to write down the Lord's words in a book, highlighting his role as the scribe of God's revelation.
Moses writes down the words of the covenant by the Lord's command, paralleling the recording in chapter 24.
Moses wrote down this law and gave it to the priests, confirming his role as the recorder of the law.
Moses completed writing the words of the law in a book, linking to the tradition of Moses as the scribe.
Instructions to build an altar for the Lord, which Moses carries out at the foot of the mountain.
Jacob erected a stone pillar as a memorial, paralleling the twelve pillars Moses set up.
Jacob raised a stone pillar at the place where God spoke to him, similar to Moses' twelve pillars.
Joshua set up twelve stones as a memorial for the twelve tribes of Israel, directly paralleling Moses' twelve pillars.
Joshua wrote the words in the book of God's law, continuing the tradition that Moses began.
Elijah built an altar with twelve stones according to the number of Jacob's sons' tribes, reflecting Moses' twelve pillars.
The Epistle to the Hebrews refers to Moses reading the words of the covenant and sprinkling blood, in connection with the covenant ceremony in Exodus 24.
Joshua 8:32 is fulfilled as a direct result of the Mosaic law written on stone in Exodus 24, linking the terms of the covenant to the entry into the promised land.
Both events use twelve stones as a symbol of the unity of Israel's twelve tribes and God's covenant with them.
Deuteronomy 5:22 confirms the divine origin of the words that Moses wrote down and for which he set up stone pillars in Exodus 24.
